To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) DIGS is a framework for security requirements engineering that supports the identification of implied goals; (ii) participants using DIGS found it easy to learn and use, and identified more implied goals than those using a standard requirements engineering tool; (iii) the overall recall of security goals for the systems was low, and the use of DIGS did not significantly improve recall.

the DIGS framework supports the discovery of security goals by providing an explicit mapping of the security goal patterns to the NIST controls, and by providing a systematic and structured way of identifying the implied security goals.
DIGS supports the discovery of a more comprehensive set of security goals, including implied goals, by providing the additional knowledge that is needed.

the elicitation of security goals and the discovery of implied security goals.
supporting analysts in security requirements elicitation by providing a systematic approach to identify a comprehensive set of goals that are relevant for the security of a software system.
supporting security requirements engineering by developing a framework that helps analysts discover security goals.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DIGS is a systematic and structured approach for discovering security goals for software systems.
DIGS is an approach to support analysts in identifying a comprehensive set of security goals for software systems.
DIGS can be used by analysts in a security requirements engineering process to discover security goals, including both explicit and implied security goals.

security requirements engineering should not be limited to the core functionality of the software system.
security goals can be elicited in a systematic and comprehensive fashion.
